lesson.title: The Engine Behind the Draw: Random Number Generators
lesson.summary: A random number generator is the tool, whether a printed table of random digits or a computer algorithm, that actually implements the chance process behind an SRS, random assignment, and every other technique in this unit that depends on genuine randomness.
lesson.body:
Every technique discussed so far, from random assignment in experiments to drawing a simple random sample, depends on having some real, working tool that produces outcomes governed by chance rather than by human choice. That tool is a random number generator. Two versions of it appear throughout statistics: a printed table of random digits, where the digits 0 through 9 appear in a long sequence such that each digit was equally likely to appear at any given position, and a computer or calculator based random number generator, which uses an algorithm to produce a sequence of digits or numbers that behaves, for practical statistical purposes, as if it were genuinely random.

Using a table of random digits requires a specific, disciplined procedure, and it is worth walking through carefully since it is a common point of error. Suppose a researcher needs to select 4 people at random from a group of 18 volunteers labeled 01 through 18. She enters the table at some starting point, reads two digits at a time, for example a stretch of the table reading 71 48 09 63 94 17 22 55, and she keeps only the two digit groups that fall between 01 and 18, discarding anything from 19 through 00 as unusable, and discarding any repeated number she has already selected. Working through that stretch, 71 is discarded, 48 is discarded, 09 is kept as her first pick, 63 is discarded, 94 is discarded, 17 is kept as her second pick, 22 is discarded, and 55 is discarded; she would continue reading further digits from the table until she has collected all 4 needed labels.

Computer and calculator based generators, such as a random integer function that produces a number from 1 to 18 on command, accomplish the same goal far more quickly, since there is no need to discard out of range values by hand, and most software can also automatically avoid repeats when sampling without replacement. Technically, most computer generated sequences are what mathematicians call pseudorandom, produced by a deterministic formula seeded with some starting value, rather than arising from a genuinely unpredictable physical process. For virtually every purpose in an introductory statistics course, this distinction does not matter, since a good pseudorandom generator passes all the same statistical tests for unpredictability and equal likelihood that a physical process like dice or a shuffled deck would pass.

What matters most, regardless of which tool is used, is that the generator gives every eligible outcome an equal chance and that the researcher applies it consistently, without stopping early because a favorable-looking pattern appeared or restarting because an unwanted number came up. That kind of interference reintroduces exactly the human judgment that random selection is designed to eliminate. Whether the numbers come from a printed table or a phone's random number app, the random number generator is the concrete engine that makes an SRS, random assignment, and every other randomized procedure in this course actually possible to carry out rather than just possible to describe.
